stem: How many times does the body of this loop run?
code:
word = "sun hat"
count = 0
for ch in word:
    count = count + 1
print(count)

options.rationale: The string has 7 characters, s, u, n, a space, h, a and t, and the loop takes each one.
This forgets that the space between the two words is a character too.
This counts the words, but looping over a string gives single characters, not words.
The loop does not take the whole string at once; it takes one character per round.

explanation: Looping over a string gives one character per round, and a space counts as a character. "sun hat" has 3 letters, 1 space and 3 more letters, so the body runs 7 times and count ends at 7.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
fruits = ("kiwi", "plum", "fig")
for f in fruits:
    last = f.upper()
print(f, last)

options.rationale: The loop variable is not reset to the first item when the loop ends; it keeps the last one.
After the loop, `f` keeps the last item it was given, "fig", and `last` holds its upper-case form.
`upper()` returns a new string for `last`; it does not change `f`.
The tuple has three items, so the last round sets `f` to "fig", not "plum".

explanation: The loop takes "kiwi", "plum" and "fig" in turn. In each round, last gets the upper-case form of f. When the loop ends, f still holds the last item, "fig", and last holds "FIG". upper() makes a new string and leaves f unchanged.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
temps = [10, 20, 30]
for t in temps:
    t = t + 5
print(temps, t)

options.rationale: Changing `t` does not change the list, and after the last round `t` holds 30 + 5.
Assigning a new value to the loop variable does not change the item in the list.
The body runs in the last round too, so `t` becomes 35 before the loop ends.
The list is unchanged, and `t` was updated to 35 in the last round.

explanation: In each round, t gets the next item and then t = t + 5 makes t refer to a new number. The list itself is never changed, so temps is still [10, 20, 30]. In the last round t is 30, then becomes 35, and it keeps that value after the loop.

stem: Which loops print exactly three lines? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: A string is looped character by character, and the space is a character, so this prints a, a space and b.
The tuple has three items, so the body runs three times.
A list is looped item by item, not word by word; it has only two items.
An empty list gives no items, so the body never runs and nothing is printed.
The list has one item, the whole word "bread", so this prints one line, not one per letter.

explanation: The body runs once per item. "a b" has three characters (a, space, b), and the tuple has three items, so both print three lines. The list ["red", "green blue"] has two items, [] has none, and ["bread"] has one.

stem: Complete the loop so the program prints `Walked 55 minutes`.
code:
total = 0
__BLANK1__ minutes __BLANK2__ [15, 30, 10]:
    total = total + minutes
print("Walked", total, "minutes")

blanks.rationale: A loop over the items of a list starts with the keyword `for`, followed by the loop variable.
`in` names the iterable that hands the items to the loop variable one by one; the other words are not part of a `for` line and give a `SyntaxError`.

explanation: A for loop has the shape for <loop variable> in <iterable>:. Each round, minutes gets the next number (15, 30, 10) and is added to total, so total ends at 55. The print is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop.
